[Exclusive] SK hynix to Begin Mass Production of LPDDR6 in Second Half; Xiaomi to Be First Customer

SK hynix plans to begin mass-producing and shipping LPDDR6, its next-generation low-power mobile DRAM, in the second half of this year. Having completed development of the product in March, the company intends to make its first shipment to China’s Xiaomi for use in mobile devices. The launch is expected to further intensify competition among the three major memory manufacturers—Samsung Electronics, SK hynix, and Micron—in SOCAMM, a next-generation, LPDDR-based low-power memory module for AI servers.

According to industry sources on July 28, SK hynix will enter full-scale mass production of LPDDR6 in the second half of this year. Xiaomi is expected to be its first customer, with the memory slated for use in the company’s next-generation flagship smartphones. SK hynix’s LPDDR6 uses its sixth-generation 10nm-class (1c) process, offering improved data-transfer speeds and power efficiency over the previous generation.

In March, SK hynix announced that it had completed certification of what it described as the world’s first LPDDR6 product, saying, “We plan to complete preparations for mass production within the first half and begin supplying the product in the second half.” Regarding the reported Xiaomi deal, however, the company said it could not confirm information related to customers.

SK hynix began doing business with Xiaomi in 2013, supplying LPDDR3 for certain models, and is understood to have continued supplying mobile DRAM through the latest LPDDR5X generation.

Samsung Electronics and SK hynix currently lead the mobile DRAM market. Meanwhile, CXMT, China’s largest memory manufacturer, has been rapidly gaining ground following its stock-market debut, bringing its market share close to that of third-ranked U.S. chipmaker Micron. Samsung supplies LPDDR to Android smartphone manufacturers worldwide, while SK hynix has a strong position among Chinese smartphone brands.

The Xiaomi deal is expected to pave the way for SK hynix to expand LPDDR6 shipments to other Chinese smartphone manufacturers, including Vivo and Oppo. Chinese smartphone makers are increasingly adopting domestically produced memory from suppliers such as CXMT in their entry-level lineups, but their flagship models—which require higher performance—remain dependent on LPDDR from the three major global memory manufacturers.

LPDDR is primarily used in mobile devices such as smartphones and tablet PCs. By reducing power consumption while maintaining high performance, it has recently experienced explosive demand from AI servers. Some industry observers expect it to become a major growth driver for the memory market after HBM, or high-bandwidth memory.

LPDDR supply prices have recently risen to levels comparable with those of DRAM, whose prices have been soaring. The increase stems from supply bottlenecks caused by memory manufacturers concentrating their production capacity on commodity DRAM and HBM.

As LPDDR applications diversify and contract prices continue to rise, memory manufacturers posted record-high revenue in the first quarter, supported by strong LPDDR sales. Market-research firm TrendForce said, “Mobile DRAM revenue increased by 64.5% in the first quarter of this year,” adding that “continued increases in contract prices will drive further growth in mobile DRAM revenue in the second quarter.”

Samsung Electronics and SK hynix are also seen as having seized the initiative by beginning preparations for mass production of the latest LPDDR6 products ahead of Micron. In January, Samsung unveiled what it described as the industry’s first LPDDR6 product built using fifth-generation 10nm-class (1b) DRAM technology. The product won a CES Innovation Award.

SK hynix’s mass production of LPDDR6 is also expected to signal the start of a full-fledged race to secure an early lead in the SOCAMM market. SOCAMM packages LPDDR into a module designed for AI servers. As the AI market shifts from training toward inference, it is rapidly emerging as a next-generation memory solution for AI servers.

In June, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang visited SK hynix’s booth at Computex 2026, Asia’s largest information-technology trade show, and left the message “LOVE SOCAMM” on a 192GB SOCAMM module.

Nvidia also recently unveiled Vera, its first internally designed CPU for AI servers. If HBM is the GPU’s natural partner, LPDDR is the CPU’s. As the AI market becomes increasingly advanced and demand for CPUs rises sharply, demand for SOCAMM is also expected to strengthen.

Samsung Expands Hwaseong Fab, Raising Production Capacity 15% by Year-End

Samsung Electronics is consolidating its DRAM production facilities at its Hwaseong campus while expanding capacity to increase the supply of commodity DRAM. The move is seen as an effort to maximize output of commodity DRAM—DDR4 prices alone have surged more than 80% in the first half of this year—and meet as much demand as possible from major technology customers such as Apple, which is considering sourcing DRAM from Chinese suppliers amid the memory shortage.

According to industry sources on the 27th, Samsung Electronics’ Memory Manufacturing Technology Center formed a task force this month and began establishing a commodity DRAM end-fab at H1, the first complex of its Hwaseong campus. The company plans to relocate end-fab equipment currently spread across H2, the campus’s second complex, and its Cheonan campus to H1, while adding production lines in the space freed up by the relocation.

An end-fab connects transistors and other memory components fabricated in the main fab and represents the final stage of front-end wafer processing. Samsung has historically expanded its Hwaseong production facilities around its main fabs, leaving some end-fab operations dispersed in Cheonan. The physical separation between the main fab and end-fab inevitably lengthened DRAM production lead times, hindering efforts to increase commodity DRAM supply.

Jun Young-hyun, head of Samsung Electronics’ Device Solutions division, recently reviewed how to use the idle cleanroom space at Hwaseong H1 created by dismantling older memory lines and ultimately selected it as the new end-fab hub. By repurposing an existing cleanroom instead of building a new fab, Samsung can reduce both capital expenditure and construction time, allowing it to expand DRAM supply more quickly.

The restructuring goes beyond simply increasing production capacity. Its key feature is the consolidation of upstream and downstream commodity DRAM production processes at a single site, significantly improving efficiency. Previously, components fabricated at the main fab in Hwaseong had to be transported to the end-fab in Cheonan for completion, creating considerable production inefficiencies. In effect, Samsung is bringing to Hwaseong the advanced production model used at its Pyeongtaek campus, where main fabs and end-fabs have been colocated since the construction stage.

“Samsung Electronics’ commodity DRAM production capacity is expected to be about 15% higher by the end of the year than it was at the beginning of the year,” an industry official said. “Bringing the main fab and end-fab together will also improve logistics efficiency by allowing wafers to be transferred collectively to downstream processing lines.”

[EXCLUSIVE] SAMSUNG’S CONTRARIAN BET: USING “CHINESE CHIPS” TO BREAK INTO CHINA’S MOBILE MARKET

As “chipflation,” or rising component prices, shakes the global semiconductor market and sharply contracts China’s smartphone market, Samsung Electronics is seriously considering using competitively priced, low-cost Chinese DRAM to target the country’s mid- and low-end smartphone segment.

According to semiconductor industry sources on July 27, Samsung Electronics is exploring a contrarian strategy of significantly reducing smartphone manufacturing costs by adopting locally sourced semiconductors, including inexpensive Chinese mobile DRAM, while substantially increasing shipments of affordable smartphones in China.

The company aims to capitalize on a market opening created as local competitors cut smartphone shipments in response to rising component prices triggered by the artificial intelligence data-center boom.

The global mobile industry has already begun to feel the effects of chipflation since the beginning of this year. Major manufacturers, including Apple, Xiaomi, Oppo, and Vivo, have either raised the prices of new products or lowered their shipment targets by approximately 15% to 20% as they struggle with mounting component-cost pressures.

Apple raised the prices of MacBooks and iPads by about $100 in June, and the market widely expects the company to increase the prices of its next-generation iPhones scheduled to launch this fall.

The bigger problem lies with Chinese smartphone makers focused on the mid- and low-end market, which lack the exceptional brand power of Apple or Huawei. Companies such as Xiaomi, Oppo, Vivo, and Honor have difficulty passing higher component costs directly on to consumers. As a result, they are voluntarily reducing production under the judgment that selling more devices would only increase their losses.

Samsung Electronics sees this situation as a potential opportunity.

While major local manufacturers hesitate under cost pressure, Samsung is considering strategically adopting lower-priced Chinese DRAM to substantially reduce its device costs. By using the resulting price competitiveness to expand supplies of affordable models such as the Galaxy A series, the company could significantly increase its share of the Chinese smartphone market, which currently stands at only about 0.6%, while also expanding the overall revenue volume of its Mobile eXperience, or MX, division.

Expectations for the MX division’s financial performance have also fallen sharply among brokerage firms, as surging memory prices driven by the AI boom have significantly increased smartphone manufacturing costs.

Several major securities firms have recently lowered their full-year earnings estimates for Samsung Electronics’ MX and Networks division or suggested that the business may have swung to an operating loss in the second quarter.

Estimated second-quarter losses include KRW 200 billion from Hana Securities, KRW 584.1 billion from Samsung Securities, KRW 1 trillion from Eugene Investment & Securities, and KRW 800 billion from iM Securities.

Samsung Securities, in particular, previously projected that the division would generate KRW 3.41 trillion in operating profit this year, but it sharply revised that estimate to an operating loss of KRW 5.841 trillion, heightening concerns over the business.

Industry experts also view Samsung Electronics’ consideration of Chinese DRAM as both a realistic and potentially significant strategic option.

Shim Woo-jung, a research fellow responsible for home appliances and digital transformation at the Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade, said, “Demand for Chinese-made DRAM is expected to increase, particularly among Chinese companies, and Apple and Samsung Electronics may also consider adopting Chinese DRAM because of cost pressures.”

He added, “With major Chinese smartphone manufacturers such as Xiaomi having significantly reduced production, Samsung Electronics could meaningfully increase its market share by expanding the supply of lower-priced smartphones such as the Galaxy A series.”

Shim also said, “Given that securities firms are estimating a possible second-quarter operating loss for Samsung Electronics’ MX division, the company is likely facing an increased sense of urgency.”

A Samsung Electronics official said the matter “could not be confirmed.”
— Jukan (@jukan05) Jul 27, 2026

items.content:
South Korea’s Meritz Securities estimates that, as part of Bain Capital’s sale of its stake in Kioxia, SK hynix’s stake in SPC1—through which it had invested alongside Bain—was also disposed of. 
As a result, Meritz projects SK hynix’s 2Q26 pretax profit at approximately KRW 100tn, including KRW 41.6tn in non-operating income. In 2018, SK hynix made a strategic investment of KRW 3.9tn through SPC1 and SPC2 in Bain Capital’s acquisition of Kioxia, formerly Toshiba Memory. 

Meritz estimates that SK hynix likely recognized cumulative gains approaching KRW 40tn upon completing the sale of SPC1 in June. Including the final SPC1 disposal gain, valuation gains on SPC2, and other investment-related gains, non-operating income is expected to exceed KRW 40tn in 2Q26. SK hynix still holds the SPC2 convertible bonds, which could convert into an approximately 14% stake in Kioxia. 

Meritz also noted that issues surrounding SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won’s divorce litigation have sharply increased the need for higher dividends from SK hynix, the group’s largest cash cow, making it highly likely that the dividends will subsequently be upstreamed through onward distributions by SK Square.
